What is a multi-currency account?

By the Ibanora teamPublished November 24, 20265 min read

In short

A multi-currency account lets you hold, receive, convert and send money in more than one currency without opening a separate bank account in each country. Some providers are banks and some are e-money firms, and in the UK that changes how your money is protected if the provider fails.

On this page

  2. How a multi-currency account works

A multi-currency account is an account that holds balances in several currencies at once. You can receive money in one currency, keep it, convert it when you choose, and send or spend it from the same place. As of November 2026, HSBC UK describes a currency account as a way to hold, send and receive money in different currencies without needing separate bank accounts in each currency. People who get paid, pay bills or travel in more than one currency use one to keep each currency apart until they need it.

What a multi-currency account is

As of November 2026, HSBC UK says currency accounts are also known as foreign currency accounts or multi-currency accounts. Whatever the name, each currency sits in its own balance, so euros stay euros until you decide to convert them, if you convert them at all.

Business providers describe the same thing in treasury terms. As of November 2026, Nium, a payments company, defines a multi-currency account as a single account structure that holds, receives and sends funds in multiple currencies, so a business does not need a separate account in each country.

How a multi-currency account works

Most multi-currency accounts do four things:

  • Hold a balance in each currency you open.
  • Receive payments into those balances, sometimes with local account details so the payer can send a domestic transfer.
  • Convert between balances when you ask.
  • Send money out, and with some providers spend it on a card.

Providers organize the balances differently. Some open a separate account for each currency under your name, and others give you one account with many balances inside it. As of November 2026, HSBC UK and Wise are examples of each, according to their own pages:

ProviderType of firmCurrenciesHow balances are organizedCard
HSBC Currency AccountBank (HSBC UK Bank plc)14A separate account for each currencyNo debit card
Wise accountNot a bank; Wise says it safeguards customer moneyOver 40One account holding many currenciesWise card available, with a fee to get one

Receiving details also vary. As of November 2026, Wise says its account can receive money from people not on Wise in 23 currencies, with local IBANs (International Bank Account Numbers) and routing numbers among the details it provides. As of November 2026, HSBC says you pay into its Currency Account by transfer from your HSBC sterling account or from another bank account.

If most of your money moves abroad rather than sitting in balances, see how cross-border payments work on their own.

Who uses a multi-currency account

As of November 2026, HSBC UK's guide says a currency account could suit you if you:

  • travel a lot
  • have a mortgage or committed bills outside the UK
  • regularly earn money outside the UK
  • plan to retire outside the UK

Businesses use them too. As of November 2026, Nium gives the example of a company that invoices clients in several currencies, holds a balance in each, pays local vendors without converting and converts only the surplus. For company use, see multi-currency business accounts. For personal use, see personal accounts.

What a multi-currency account costs

Costs come from account fees, payment fees and currency conversion. As of November 2026, HSBC UK's guide warns that some currency accounts charge monthly account fees or payment fees, and some make you keep a minimum amount in each currency or pay extra.

As of November 2026, HSBC says its Currency Account has no monthly account fee and charges nothing to send money to another HSBC account, while fees may apply when you send to a non-HSBC account outside the UK. As of November 2026, HSBC converts at the HSBC Exchange Rate, which it says includes a currency conversion charge.

Wise says, as of November 2026, that its account is free to open with no subscription, and that it charges fees when you send, spend or receive money if there is a conversion, to get a Wise card, or to turn on Wise Assets.

Conversion is where costs hide. A provider can charge a visible fee, a markup built into its exchange rate, or both. As an example, on a $1,000 conversion, a 1% markup on the exchange rate costs $10. Comparing a provider's rate with the mid-market rate on the same day shows the markup. The Wise vs Revolut comparison sets out how those two providers charge for conversion.

Is a multi-currency account safe? Banks and e-money firms

In the UK, the answer depends on what kind of firm holds your money. The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) says that if a non-bank payment provider goes out of business, your money will not be protected by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme (FSCS). Electronic money institutions (EMIs) and authorised payment institutions (APIs) protect it through a process called safeguarding instead.

The FCA sets out the difference by provider type on its page Using payment service providers:

Provider typeFSCS protectionRequired to safeguardComplaints to the Financial Ombudsman
Bank or building societyYesNoYes
Electronic money institution (EMI)NoYesYes
Authorised payment institution (API)NoYesYes
Small payment institution (SPI)NoNoYes

For banks, the FSCS says it compensates up to £120,000 per eligible person, per UK-authorised bank, building society or credit union, a limit that rose to that level on December 1, 2025. Banks in the same group that share a banking license count as one bank for that limit. As of November 2026, HSBC UK's guide says a currency account with an authorised UK bank is protected under the FSCS, with up to £240,000 for joint accounts.

Safeguarding works differently. The FCA says EMIs and APIs must either put your money in a separate safeguarding account with a bank, or protect it with an insurance policy or similar guarantee. If the firm fails, you should get most of your money back, but it may take time and may not be the full amount, because the administrator or liquidator of the firm could take some costs.

The FCA also suggests checking its Financial Services Register. Some providers trade under a brand name, so look for the company operating behind it, usually named at the bottom of the provider's website or in its terms and conditions.

How to open a multi-currency account

  1. List the currencies you need. As of November 2026, HSBC UK's guide points out that a currency account will not cover every currency.
  2. Find out what kind of firm the provider is, using the company name in its terms and, in the UK, the FCA register.
  3. Check eligibility. As of November 2026, HSBC says you must be 18 or over and hold an active HSBC current account (not a Basic Bank Account) to apply for its Currency Account.
  4. Read the fee page for account, payment and conversion charges, and any minimum balance.
  5. Check what comes with the account: local account details, a card, and whether you can pay in or take out cash.

Questions

What is the difference between a multi-currency account and a foreign currency account?

As of November 2026, Nium says a foreign currency account typically holds a single non-domestic currency, while a multi-currency account holds several currencies at once. As of November 2026, HSBC UK uses the names interchangeably and says currency accounts are also known as foreign currency accounts or multi-currency accounts. Check what the specific account holds rather than relying on the name.

Is a multi-currency account a bank account?

Only if the provider is a bank. The FCA says electronic money institutions can also provide non-bank current accounts, and money held with them is safeguarded instead of being covered by the FSCS. The provider's terms and the FCA register show which kind of firm you are dealing with.

Does a multi-currency account pay interest?

It depends on the provider and the account. As of November 2026, HSBC UK says no interest is payable on its Currency Account. Check the provider's own account page for any interest feature and its conditions.

Does a multi-currency account come with a card?

Some do and some do not. As of November 2026, HSBC UK says its Currency Account does not come with a debit card, while Wise offers a Wise card and lists a fee to get one.
